text:
The University of Melbourne was established in 1853 as a result of a proposal by Hugh Childers, with a foundation stone laid in 1854. It began with three professors and 16 students, offering degrees in arts, medicine, law, and music. The university expanded significantly in the early 20th century, establishing a law school in 1857, a faculty of engineering in 1861, and a school of medicine in 1862. Residential colleges were first opened in 1872, divided among the four main Christian denominations.
In the 1900s, the university expanded its offerings to include more utilitarian courses, such as the Diploma of Education in 1903. The university became a leader in research, emerging as a prominent institution in Australia. In the 1980s and 1990s, it amalgamated with several tertiary colleges, including the Melbourne Teachers' College in 1988 and the Victorian College of the Arts in 1992. In 2001, the Melbourne School of Population Health was established, the first of its kind in Australia.
In 2008, Vice-Chancellor Glyn Davis introduced the "Melbourne Model," replacing traditional undergraduate specialist degrees with a two-degree undergraduate/graduate structure. This model was controversial, with criticism over job and subject cuts and a perceived risk of "dumbing down" content. In 2013–2015, Davis introduced a wide-reaching restructuring of the university's administration, known as the Business Improvement Program, which led to the sacking of 500 administrative staff. The university also embarked on a large capital works program, spending $2 billion on new buildings across campuses.
In 2020, the university faced criticism over its handling of student mental health, including the high number of student suicides and the university's failure to provide adequate mental health resources. In response, the university implemented new safety measures and increased funding for student wellbeing. In 2021, the university was involved in a major controversy over its handling of student protests, including a protest over investments in Israeli government companies and bonds. The university was found to have breached student privacy by using location data to identify protest participants.
The university has three campuses: Parkville (the primary campus), Southbank (home to the Victorian College of the Arts and the Melbourne Conservatorium of Music), and Burnley (dedicated to horticulture). The Parkville campus includes historic buildings such as the Old Quad and Baldwin Spencer buildings, and has undergone restoration and modernization. The Southbank campus is a hub for creative arts and music, with a state-of-the-art conservatorium and performance spaces. The Burnley campus features nine hectares of heritage-listed gardens and offers short courses, associate degrees, and postgraduate studies.
The university is governed by a University Council, which includes the chancellor, vice-chancellor, and academic board. The academic board oversees teaching, research, and learning, and is responsible for academic policy. The university has nine faculties, including the Faculty of Arts, Faculty of Business and Economics, Faculty of Education, Faculty of Engineering and Information Technology, Faculty of Fine Arts and Music, Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry and Health Sciences, Faculty of Science, and Faculty of Law.
The University of Melbourne has a strong academic reputation, ranking among the top universities in Australia and globally. In the 2024 Aggregate Ranking of Top Universities, it achieved a position of #23 (1st nationally). It is ranked #6 in the Australian Financial Review Best Universities Ranking 2024 and #19 in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2025. The university is known for its research output, with a strong emphasis on biomedical science, physical science, engineering, nanoscience, material science, information technology, humanities, and social sciences.
The university has a diverse student body, with international students making up 44% of the student population. The university offers a wide range of undergraduate and postgraduate programs, including 17 undergraduate and postgraduate degrees. The university has a strong focus on student engagement, with over 200 clubs and societies, including cultural, course-related, political, language exchange, spiritual, and community-focused groups. The university also hosts a range of student events, including the annual "Getting to Know the University of Melbourne" event, which is open to high school students.
The University of Melbourne has produced many notable alumni, including Nobel laureates, politicians, scientists, artists, and entrepreneurs. Notable alumni include Elizabeth Blackburn, a Nobel Prize-winning biologist; Peter Singer, a prominent philosopher; and Cate Blanchett, an acclaimed actress. The university has a strong commitment to research and innovation, with over 3,000 research staff and more than 100 research centers and institutes. The university has a strong international presence, with partnerships and exchange programs with over 250 overseas institutions. The university also has a strong focus on sustainability, with initiatives to reduce carbon emissions and promote environmental responsibility.
